doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Learning orchestration and writing chamber works
summary: Levy taught himself orchestration through playing many instruments and attending concerts, and mentions Harmonia Mundi, an oboe sonata and Eugene Friesen.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. How did you learn about the – all the things you need to know about ranges and what instruments can do well and not so well. Like basically orchestration. Did you teach yourself? © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

Yeah. And just also from knowing how to play a lot of instruments, that kind of helps. You know I can play clarinet and flute and I know what the oboe is and I know what the range of trumpets are. I mean I’ve played with trumpet players for years, and trombone, and I know what these things sound like you know. I don’t really write out of range. And I do play mandolin and my ex-girlfriend was a violinist, and so I know, I mean I’m a pretty good mandolin player so I’m not going to write unplayable things for strings. I mean I know how to write the correct double stops and all that stuff, and working a lot with Eugene Friesen, the great cellist within that band Trio Globo. It familiarized me with the cello on a very personal level, and I play some bass too so I understand bass. So learning the instruments really helped me with the orchestration, and going to a lot of live concerts of Chicago Symphony also helped me greatly. Before I wrote the concerto I wrote a chamber suite that’s also on the same album that’s in 1995, for oboe, flute, violin, viola, cello and me, and I really like that piece. I don't know if you’ve heard it but it’s called “Harmonia Mundi” and it’s really good. I’m very proud of it. And I also composed an oboe sonata about ten years ago which was just recorded by an oboist named Jared Hauser. Did a real nice job with it.
